Fi1wkUczuyk.gist: The three financial statements together reveal a business's health: what it owns, what it earns, and its cash.
points: The balance sheet is a snapshot at one date; assets always equal liabilities plus equity (the accounting equation).
The income statement covers a period: revenue minus expenses equals net profit (e.g. $255M - $248M = $7M).
The cash flow statement tracks cash inflows and outflows, reconciling opening to closing cash on the balance sheet.
Cash-method accounting records revenue when cash is received; accrual recognizes revenue when earned, expenses when incurred.
Profit doesn't equal cash flow, which is why accrual businesses must prepare a separate cash flow statement.

CMv1zlZhb4Q.gist: Build a balance sheet from a trial balance, but remember revenue and expenses roll into retained earnings.
points: A balance sheet is built from an adjusted trial balance, where total debits must equal total credits.
Current assets (receivables, prepaids) are short-term; non-current assets split into tangible and intangible.
The common mistake: forgetting that revenue and expense accounts flow into retained earnings within equity.
Retained earnings equals opening retained earnings minus dividends plus current-year net profit.
Equity has two parts: capital contributions (common stock) and retained earnings (accumulated profits).

hrSUq4wcd0g.gist: The income statement reveals multiple profit layers, and gross margin trends expose hidden cost or pricing problems.
points: Direct costs (cost of goods sold) are variable and trace to products; indirect costs (overheads) are often fixed.
Revenue minus direct costs equals gross profit; minus overheads equals operating profit (EBIT).
Operating profit is EBIT; subtracting interest and tax gives net profit, the bottom line.
Gross profit margin = (sales - COGS) / sales; in the example it fell from 70% to 64% despite higher sales.
Comparing line items across periods lets accountants build a narrative explaining what drove the changes.

0--AvwZabIQ.gist: Make an income statement by pulling revenue and categorized expenses from a trial balance below the line.
points: The detailed income statement layers operating revenue, cost of sales, overheads, then interest and tax.
An adjusted trial balance separates balance-sheet accounts (above the line) from revenue and expenses (below).
Basic version: revenue $60M minus expenses $50.35M leaves $9.65M net profit.
Cost of sales is a direct operating cost; general, selling, marketing, depreciation are indirect operating costs.
Watch depreciation: if assets aren't used in operations, that depreciation becomes a non-operating cost instead.

_VS4ni14JHs.gist: Five balance-sheet numbers let you judge a company's financial health in seconds, like Chipotle's debt-free fortress.
points: Assets are listed by liquidity; current assets convert to cash within a year, long-term assets benefit longer.
Goodwill is the cumulative premium paid for acquisitions; a large figure signals an acquisitive, riskier strategy.
The five key numbers: cash plus securities, total debt, goodwill, retained earnings, and treasury stock.
Treasury stock (negative) shows buybacks; Chipotle's -$5B means it actively returns capital to shareholders.
Chipotle had ~$1.9B cash and zero debt, making it a 'financial fortress' on quick inspection.

Q0o9S0q0Rr4.gist: Read the MD&A across many years, but the business and risk sections only once, to value a company.
points: Find 10-Ks via 'company name + investor relations' or the SEC's annual filings; Form 10-K is the annual report.
Item 1 Business explains how the company makes and spends money (e.g. Texas Roadhouse spends ~$5.2M per new restaurant).
Risk factors list what could prevent your investment from delivering the expected return; read them thoroughly once.
MD&A is the most important section, explaining what drove success or failure and management's future strategy.
Notes to financial statements serve as a glossary; skip the ~100 pages of employment-agreement legal jargon.

BQHILdryQ_o.gist: Buffett buys when a company is obviously cheap from the annual report alone, skipping due diligence theater.
points: Buffett invested $500M in PetroChina in 2002-03 reading only the annual report, no management contact or broker reports.
He valued PetroChina at ~$100B while it traded near $35B, so further precision was a waste of time.
His test: you only need to know someone is 'fat,' not their exact weight; the gap must hit you between the eyes.
If you can't decide from the figures alone, don't bother digging deeper; conventional due diligence rarely prevents mistakes.
Munger: thinking like engineers with margins of reliability beats paying fees for fine-grained third-party judgments.

7OjsEF04V8o.gist: Use common-size analysis, converting statement lines to percentages, to compare a company across years and rivals.
points: Start with the Business section to understand the company, then decide whether to eliminate or keep analyzing it.
MD&A explains performance and segments; pairing it with the earnings call reveals management's tone and reactions.
Common-size analysis converts items to percentages (e.g. Apple's products were ~82% of revenue, declining over years).
On the income statement use total revenue as the base; on the balance sheet use total assets.
The current ratio compares current liabilities to current assets; footnotes explain unusual line items.

qM2_RlUb3jc.gist: A 10-K has four parts and items numbered 1-16; focus on business, financials, and MD&A.
points: 3M's 2017 10-K ran 176 pages, much of it exhibits like incentive plans the speaker never reads.
Priority reads: Item 1 Business, Item 6 selected financial data, Item 8 financial statements, then Item 7 MD&A.
Item 6 gives a five-year comparison of sales, net income, EPS, and debt to spot longer-term trends.
Item 9 disagreements with accountants and Item 1B unresolved staff comments are red flags worth studying carefully.
Parts III items (compensation, governance) are usually deferred to the separate proxy statement by reference.

3bgBeIZI0c0.gist: Read five 10-K sections; the biggest red flag is a business being disrupted despite beautiful financials.
points: The five sections to read: business, risk factors, MD&A, financial statements with footnotes, and executive compensation.
Read Business first since you can't invest in what you don't understand; risk factors reveal how you could lose money.
Beware boilerplate risks; focus on risks specific to the company (e.g. Alphabet's ~98% reliance on advertising).
Bed Bath & Beyond had beautiful financials but flat shares for a decade because e-commerce disrupted it.
Check related-party transactions in footnotes, where insiders can siphon money; review at least five to ten years.
